dx: Classic homocystinuria with downward lens dislocation
case: A 13-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of blurred vision. He has needed special education services since early childhood. He is at the 98th percentile for height, and his arm span exceeds his height by 6 cm. His fingers are long and thin, and his cheeks are flushed. Slit-lamp examination shows bilateral inferonasal subluxation of the lenses. The thoracic spine curves to the right, and forward bending shows a prominent right posterior rib hump. Plasma total homocysteine concentration is 190 micromol/L (normal 5 to 15), and plasma methionine concentration is 410 micromol/L (normal 10 to 40). Echocardiography shows a normal aortic root. Diagnosis: classic homocystinuria from cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency.

questions.stem: He is scheduled for removal of both lenses under general anesthesia. Without specific preventive measures, which of the following perioperative complications is this patient at greatest risk for?
options: Acute dissection of the ascending aorta
Malignant hyperthermia from anesthetic agents
Venous thrombosis with pulmonary embolism
Spontaneous pneumothorax from apical blebs
approach: Recognize the disorder: Marfan-like build, downward lens subluxation, intellectual disability, and very high homocysteine point to homocystinuria.
Recall the main danger in homocystinuria: high homocysteine damages endothelium and promotes arterial and venous clots.
Surgery and immobilization add to that clotting risk, so thromboembolism is the complication to expect.
questions.why: Thromboembolism is the leading cause of serious illness and death in untreated homocystinuria. High homocysteine injures endothelium and promotes platelet and clotting activity, so both veins and arteries can clot. Surgery, anesthesia, and bed rest add stasis and raise the risk further, which is why these patients need careful clot prevention around procedures. Aortic root dilation and dissection are the main threats in Marfan syndrome, and his normal aortic root fits homocystinuria.
whyNot: Aortic root dilation and dissection are the classic cardiovascular complications of Marfan syndrome. His aortic root is normal, and dissection is not a typical feature of homocystinuria.
Malignant hyperthermia is linked to RYR1 mutations and some myopathies. It has no link to homocystinuria.
Correct.
Spontaneous pneumothorax from apical blebs is a feature of Marfan syndrome, from weak connective tissue in the lung. It is not the major perioperative risk in homocystinuria.

questions.stem: A cousin of this patient has Marfan syndrome inherited from her father. She carries one normal FBN1 allele and one FBN1 missense allele. Which of the following best explains why one abnormal allele is enough to cause her disease?
options: Mutant fibrillin-1 disrupts microfibrils containing normal protein
Half-normal enzyme activity is too low to process the substrate
The normal allele is silenced by parent-of-origin imprinting
A later somatic mutation inactivates the normal allele in aortic tissue
approach: Note the inheritance: one mutant FBN1 allele causes disease, so Marfan syndrome is autosomal dominant.
Ask what kind of protein fibrillin-1 is. It is a structural protein that polymerizes into microfibrils.
In a polymer, abnormal subunits disturb the whole assembly, so the mutant protein spoils the normal protein's work (a dominant negative effect).
questions.why: Marfan syndrome is autosomal dominant. Fibrillin-1 molecules join end to end and side by side to form microfibrils. A missense mutant protein is built into the same microfibrils as the normal protein and disrupts them, so the tissue behaves as if most fibrillin were defective. This is a dominant negative effect, typical of structural proteins. The defective microfibrils also fail to hold TGF-beta, adding excess TGF-beta signaling. Homocystinuria differs: it is an autosomal recessive enzyme deficiency.
whyNot: Correct.
Fibrillin-1 is a structural protein, not an enzyme. Most enzyme deficiencies are recessive because about half of normal enzyme activity is enough, which is the pattern of homocystinuria.
Imprinting makes disease depend on which parent passed the gene, as in Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes. FBN1 is not imprinted.

A second somatic hit that removes the normal allele is the model for tumor suppressor genes, such as RB1. In Marfan syndrome the mutation is present in every cell from conception, and no second hit is needed.

questions.stem: Homocysteine is thought to damage fibrillin-1 by reacting with its many disulfide-bonded cysteine residues, which may explain why this patient's skeletal and lens findings resemble Marfan syndrome. In normal elastic tissue, such as the ligamentum flavum, intact fibrillin-1 microfibrils regulate growth factor signaling by which of the following?
options: Presenting fibroblast growth factor to receptors on chondrocytes
Cleaving latent TGF-beta from its binding protein to activate it
Degrading TGF-beta through bound matrix metalloproteinases
Holding latent TGF-beta inactive in the extracellular matrix
approach: Recall the structure of an elastic fiber: an elastin core laid on a scaffold of fibrillin-1 microfibrils.
Recall the second job of fibrillin-1: it binds the large latent complex of TGF-beta and stores it in the matrix.
Predict the effect of damaged fibrillin: latent TGF-beta is released and activated, so signaling increases.
questions.why: Elastic fibers, abundant in the ligamentum flavum and the aortic wall, have an elastin core built on fibrillin-1 microfibrils. Besides acting as a scaffold, fibrillin-1 binds TGF-beta in its latent form (with latency-associated peptide and latent TGF-beta binding protein) and keeps it stored in the matrix. When fibrillin-1 is defective, more TGF-beta is freed and activated. Excess TGF-beta signaling contributes to aortic root dilation and other features of Marfan syndrome.
whyNot: Fibroblast growth factor signaling in chondrocytes is the pathway altered in achondroplasia (FGFR3). Fibrillin-1 is known for binding TGF-beta.
Fibrillin-1 stores latent TGF-beta. Release and activation happen when microfibrils are defective or when other proteins act on the complex, so this reverses its role.
Matrix metalloproteinases remodel matrix proteins. Fibrillin-1 does not control TGF-beta by degrading it.
Correct.

questions.stem: Over the next 3 years, his thoracic curve progresses to 95 degrees. Which of the following best describes this spinal deformity and its most likely effect on his pulmonary function?
options: Lateral curve without vertebral rotation; normal lung volumes at rest
Lateral curve with vertebral rotation; reduced total lung capacity
Lateral curve with vertebral rotation; reduced FEV1/FVC ratio
Exaggerated thoracic kyphosis; increased total lung capacity
approach: Identify the deformity: a lateral thoracic curve with a rib hump on forward bending is scoliosis, and the rib hump means the vertebrae are rotated.
Link structure to function: a severe curve twists the rib cage and stiffens the chest wall, so the lungs cannot fully expand.
A stiff chest wall gives a restrictive pattern: low total lung capacity with a normal or high FEV1/FVC ratio.
questions.why: Structural scoliosis is a lateral curvature of the spine combined with vertebral rotation. The rotation carries the ribs backward on the convex side, which forms the rib hump seen on forward bending. Thoracic curves over about 70 degrees distort the rib cage and reduce chest wall compliance. The result is a restrictive defect, with reduced total lung capacity and vital capacity, and in severe cases hypoventilation and pulmonary hypertension.
whyNot: A curve without rotation is a nonstructural (functional) curve, such as from a leg length difference, and it does not cause a rib hump. A 95-degree curve also impairs lung expansion.
Correct.
A low FEV1/FVC ratio is the obstructive pattern of asthma or COPD. Chest wall deformity limits lung volume but does not narrow the airways.
Excessive thoracic kyphosis is a forward curve seen in the sagittal plane, as with vertebral compression fractures. His curve is lateral, and chest wall deformity lowers lung volumes.

dx: Septic arthritis of the hip in an infant
case: A 9-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of fever and irritability for 2 days. She cries when her diaper is changed and has not moved her right leg since this morning. She was born at term and has been healthy. Her temperature is 39.3 °C (102.7 °F), pulse is 168/min, respirations are 36/min, and blood pressure is 92/54 mm Hg. The right hip is held flexed, abducted, and externally rotated, and any passive movement of it makes her cry. Leukocyte count is 22,400/mm3 (normal for age 6,000 to 17,500), erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 68 mm/h (normal 0 to 10), and C-reactive protein is 11.2 mg/dL (normal under 1.0). Ultrasonography shows a large right hip effusion. Diagnosis: septic arthritis of the right hip.

questions.stem: Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. MRI shows a small abscess in the proximal femoral metaphysis. The skin of the groin and thigh is normal, and there is no inguinal lymphadenopathy. Which of the following best explains how the infection most likely reached the joint?
options: Lymphatic spread from suppurative inguinal lymphadenitis
Contiguous spread from cellulitis of the overlying groin skin
Ascending spread along the sheath of the femoral nerve
Rupture of metaphyseal osteomyelitis into the joint cavity
approach: Identify the route of entry: bacteremia with a metaphyseal abscess means the bacteria first seeded bone through the blood.
Recall the anatomy: the proximal femoral metaphysis lies inside the hip joint capsule.
Pus that breaks through the thin metaphyseal cortex therefore drains straight into the joint.
questions.why: Most septic arthritis is hematogenous, and Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause in children. In children, blood-borne bacteria settle in the metaphysis, where blood flow is slow. The hip capsule attaches below the femoral neck, so the proximal femoral metaphysis is inside the joint. When pus breaks through the thin cortex, it enters the joint directly. In infants, vessels that cross the growth plate also let infection reach the epiphysis and joint. The shoulder, elbow, and ankle share this intracapsular metaphysis risk.
whyNot: Suppurative lymphadenitis would cause tender, enlarged inguinal nodes, which she does not have. Lymphatic spread into a joint is not a usual route.
Contiguous spread from cellulitis can infect a superficial joint or bursa, as in prepatellar bursitis. Her skin is normal, and the hip is deep.
Nerve sheaths are not a route of bacterial spread to joints. Infection travels along nerves mainly with viruses such as herpes simplex or rabies.
Correct.

topics: Pathogenesis of septic arthritis in children

questions.stem: A nerve injury is considered as a cause of her refusal to move the leg. In the early lower limb bud, the L4 spinal segment supplies the cranial (preaxial) border, and S1 supplies the caudal (postaxial) border. After normal limb rotation, which of the following dermatome positions results?
options: L4 on the lateral leg and S1 on the medial foot
L4 on the medial leg and S1 on the lateral foot
L4 on the posterior calf and S1 on the great toe
L4 on the anterior shin and S1 on the dorsal foot
approach: Recall the direction of rotation: the lower limb rotates medially about 90 degrees during development.
Apply it to the borders: the preaxial (L4) border turns to face medially, and the postaxial (S1) border turns laterally.
So L4 lies along the medial leg toward the great toe side, and S1 lies along the lateral foot and little toe.
questions.why: Limb buds start with a cranial preaxial border and a caudal postaxial border. The lower limb rotates medially, so the preaxial border, with the great toe and the L4 dermatome, ends up on the medial side. The postaxial border, with the little toe and S1, ends up laterally. Because the leg also extends and twists, the dermatomes spiral down the limb: L4 on the medial leg, L5 on the anterolateral leg and dorsum of the foot, and S1 on the lateral foot and heel.
whyNot: This is the reverse of normal. It would result from lateral rotation, which is the direction the upper limb turns.
Correct.
The posterior calf is supplied mainly by S1 and S2, and the great toe by L5. L4 is not posterior after medial rotation.
The dorsum of the foot is mainly L5 territory, and S1 lies on the lateral and plantar foot. The anterior shin is shared by L4 and L5.

questions.stem: Developmental dysplasia of the hip was briefly considered. Which of the following findings, if present in this infant, would most support developmental dysplasia over her current diagnosis?
options: Painless limited abduction with apparent thigh shortening
Hip held flexed, abducted, and externally rotated
Fragmented, flattened ossific nucleus of the femoral head
Posterior slip of the capital epiphysis on the neck
approach: Separate the hip disorders by age and pain: septic arthritis is acute, painful, and febrile; developmental dysplasia is painless.
Recall how dysplasia shows after the newborn period: Ortolani and Barlow signs fade as soft tissues tighten, so limited abduction and a short thigh become the signs.
Match the other findings to their disorders: femoral head fragmentation is Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, and epiphyseal slip is slipped capital femoral epiphysis.
questions.why: Developmental dysplasia of the hip is a painless instability or dislocation present from birth. In newborns it is found with the Ortolani (reduction clunk) and Barlow (dislocation) maneuvers. By about 3 months these signs usually disappear, and a dislocated hip shows limited abduction, asymmetric thigh folds, and apparent shortening of the thigh (Galeazzi sign). Fever and a painful hip held in flexion, abduction, and external rotation point to a joint effusion, as in septic arthritis.
whyNot: Correct.
This position maximizes joint capsule volume and is how a child holds a hip with an effusion, as in septic arthritis or transient synovitis. It does not suggest dysplasia.
Fragmentation and flattening of the femoral head epiphysis are signs of Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, an osteonecrosis of children aged about 4 to 10 years.
Posterior slip of the capital epiphysis is slipped capital femoral epiphysis, a disorder of obese adolescents during the growth spurt.

questions.stem: Aspiration of the hip yields cloudy yellow fluid. The leukocyte count is 112,000/mm3 (noninflammatory fluid under 2,000) with 93% neutrophils. No crystals are seen, and the Gram stain shows no organisms. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of these results?
options: Inflammatory fluid consistent with reactive arthritis
Inflammatory fluid consistent with juvenile idiopathic arthritis
Septic fluid in spite of a negative Gram stain
Hemorrhagic fluid consistent with occult trauma
approach: Classify by leukocyte count: under 2,000 is noninflammatory, about 2,000 to 50,000 is inflammatory, and over about 50,000 with mostly neutrophils is septic until proven otherwise.
Weigh the Gram stain: it misses organisms in a large share of true joint infections, so a negative stain does not rule out infection.
Combine with the clinical picture: fever, high inflammatory markers, and a count over 100,000 mean septic arthritis.
questions.why: A synovial leukocyte count above about 50,000/mm3 with mostly neutrophils is the septic range, and counts above 100,000 are especially specific. The Gram stain is negative in roughly a third to half of culture-proven septic arthritis, and fastidious organisms such as Kingella kingae in young children are often missed by stain and routine culture. A negative stain therefore cannot overrule a septic cell count in a febrile child. The joint still needs drainage and antibiotics.
whyNot: Reactive arthritis gives inflammatory fluid, usually well under 50,000 cells, and it follows a distant infection by 1 to 4 weeks. It also typically affects older children and adults.
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis gives inflammatory fluid and requires arthritis for at least 6 weeks. It does not explain an acute febrile illness with over 100,000 cells.
Correct.
Hemorrhagic fluid is bloody with many red cells, as after trauma or in hemophilia. This fluid is cloudy and yellow with a very high neutrophil count.

dx: Parvovirus B19 polyarthritis in an elementary school teacher
case: A 34-year-old woman who teaches first grade comes to the physician because of a 6-day history of painful swelling of both hands, wrists, and knees with about 30 minutes of morning stiffness. Two weeks ago she had low-grade fever, headache, and malaise that resolved within a few days. Several children in her class recently had bright red cheeks followed by a lacy rash on the arms. She received the MMR vaccine in childhood. Her temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F). There is symmetric tenderness and swelling of the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, wrists, and knees. Hemoglobin concentration is 11.8 g/dL (normal 12 to 16), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 34 mm/h (normal 0 to 20). Rheumatoid factor is negative. Hand radiographs show soft tissue swelling without erosions. Diagnosis: parvovirus B19 associated polyarthritis.

questions.stem: Which of the following serologic results would best confirm the cause of her arthritis?
options: Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody
IgM antibody to parvovirus B19
IgG antibody to rubella virus
Elevated antistreptolysin O titer
approach: Place the illness: symmetric small joint arthritis in an adult after exposure to children with fifth disease is postinfectious arthritis from parvovirus B19.
Choose the test that shows recent infection: IgM antibodies appear early and fade over a few months.
Set aside tests that show past immunity or other diseases.
questions.why: Parvovirus B19 causes fifth disease (erythema infectiosum) in children. Adults, especially women, often have no rash but develop an acute, symmetric arthritis of the hands, wrists, and knees that can mimic rheumatoid arthritis. It is usually self-limited over weeks and does not erode bone. IgM antibody to parvovirus B19 confirms recent infection. IgG alone shows past infection and is present in many adults.
whyNot: Anti-CCP antibody is highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis, which her arthritis can resemble. It would point away from a postviral cause.
Correct.
Rubella IgG is expected after her childhood MMR vaccine, so it shows immunity, not recent infection. Rubella and rubella vaccine can cause arthritis in women, but this would not confirm it.
An elevated antistreptolysin O titer supports recent group A streptococcal infection, as in rheumatic fever with migratory large joint arthritis. Her exposure and joint pattern fit parvovirus.

questions.stem: Her symptoms resolve over 4 weeks. Her 31-year-old sister has had 2 years of polyarthritis, Raynaud phenomenon, diffusely swollen fingers, and proximal muscle weakness with an elevated serum creatine kinase. Which of the following antibodies is most likely to be present in the sister?
options: Anti-centromere antibody
Anti-double-stranded DNA antibody
Anti-topoisomerase I (Scl-70) antibody
Anti-U1 ribonucleoprotein antibody
approach: Sort the sister's findings: arthritis suggests lupus, Raynaud phenomenon and swollen fingers suggest scleroderma, and proximal weakness with high creatine kinase suggests myositis.
Features of three connective tissue diseases in one patient define mixed connective tissue disease.
Recall its marker: high titers of anti-U1 RNP antibody.
questions.why: Mixed connective tissue disease combines features of SLE (arthritis, sometimes rash), systemic sclerosis (Raynaud phenomenon, puffy swollen hands, esophageal dysmotility), and polymyositis (proximal weakness, high creatine kinase). The defining antibody is a high titer of anti-U1 ribonucleoprotein. The arthritis is usually nonerosive, like the arthritis of SLE. Pulmonary hypertension is an important cause of death.
whyNot: Anti-centromere antibody marks limited systemic sclerosis (CREST). It does not explain myositis and polyarthritis.
Anti-dsDNA antibody is specific for SLE and tracks with lupus nephritis. Myositis and swollen fingers point to an overlap disease.
Anti-Scl-70 marks diffuse systemic sclerosis with widespread skin thickening and interstitial lung disease, not this overlap pattern.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her 66-year-old mother has had hand pain for several years. The pain worsens with use and improves with rest, and morning stiffness lasts about 10 minutes. Which of the following findings is most likely on examination of the mother's hands?
options: Soft swelling of the metacarpophalangeal joints
Ulnar deviation at the metacarpophalangeal joints
Bony enlargement of the distal interphalangeal joints
Firm subcutaneous nodules over the extensor surface of the forearm
approach: Identify the mother's disorder: pain with use, relief with rest, and brief stiffness in an older adult mean osteoarthritis.
Recall the joint distribution: osteoarthritis of the hand favors the DIP and PIP joints and the base of the thumb, and spares the MCP joints.
The bony DIP swellings are Heberden nodes (PIP swellings are Bouchard nodes).
questions.why: Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease of older adults. In the hand it affects the distal interphalangeal joints, the proximal interphalangeal joints, and the first carpometacarpal joint. Osteophytes produce hard bony enlargements: Heberden nodes at the DIP joints and Bouchard nodes at the PIP joints. Rheumatoid arthritis, which the daughter's arthritis resembles, is a soft tissue synovitis of the MCP and PIP joints that spares the DIP joints and causes more than 1 hour of morning stiffness.
whyNot: Soft, boggy MCP swelling is synovitis, typical of rheumatoid arthritis and of the daughter's viral arthritis. Osteoarthritis usually spares the MCP joints.
Ulnar deviation comes from long-standing rheumatoid synovitis that loosens the MCP capsule and lets the extensor tendons slip toward the ulnar side.
Correct.
Rheumatoid nodules over the extensor forearm occur in seropositive rheumatoid arthritis. They are not a feature of osteoarthritis.

questions.stem: Her physician explains that her arthritis should resolve without joint damage, whereas rheumatoid arthritis, which it can resemble, is associated with HLA-DR4. Which of the following best explains how this allele increases the risk of rheumatoid arthritis?
options: Its peptide groove presents citrullinated peptides to CD4+ T cells
It encodes the enzyme that converts arginine residues to citrulline
Its molecules present viral peptides to cytotoxic CD8+ T cells in synovium
It lowers complement levels and impairs clearance of immune complexes
approach: Recall what HLA-DR is: an MHC class II molecule that presents peptides to CD4+ helper T cells.
Recall the autoantigen in rheumatoid arthritis: citrullinated self-proteins.
Connect them: the HLA-DR4 shared epitope binds citrullinated peptides well, so helper T cells are activated against them.
questions.why: HLA-DR4 (HLA-DRB1 alleles carrying the shared epitope) is the main genetic risk factor for rheumatoid arthritis. These MHC class II molecules bind citrullinated peptides with high affinity and present them to CD4+ T cells. The activated helper T cells drive B cells to make anti-CCP antibodies and drive synovial macrophages to release TNF, IL-1, and IL-6. The result is chronic synovitis and pannus that erodes cartilage and bone.
whyNot: Correct.
Peptidylarginine deiminase (PAD) enzymes convert arginine to citrulline. They are not encoded in the HLA region, and HLA-DR4 is a peptide-presenting molecule.
HLA-DR is MHC class II, which presents to CD4+ T cells. CD8+ T cells recognize peptides on MHC class I molecules such as HLA-B27.
Inherited deficiency of early complement proteins such as C1q, C2, or C4 impairs immune complex clearance and raises the risk of SLE, not rheumatoid arthritis through HLA-DR4.

dx: Clostridium perfringens gas gangrene after a gunshot wound to the thigh
case: A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 hours after a gunshot wound to the left thigh. The wound was irrigated and sutured closed at an urgent care clinic, and radiographs at that time showed retained bullet fragments in the quadriceps. Over the past 6 hours he has developed rapidly worsening, severe thigh pain. His temperature is 38.3 °C (100.9 °F), pulse is 132/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 88/56 mm Hg. The thigh is tense and swollen, with bronze discoloration, hemorrhagic bullae, and crepitus extending well above the wound. The wound drains thin, brown, foul-smelling fluid. Serum creatine kinase activity is 14,200 U/L (normal 30 to 200). Radiographs show gas dissecting through the quadriceps muscles. Diagnosis: Clostridium perfringens gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis).

questions.stem: A Gram stain of necrotic muscle obtained at surgery shows large, blunt-ended gram-positive rods and very few neutrophils despite extensive tissue destruction. Which of the following best explains the scarcity of neutrophils?
options: Alpha toxin lysing leukocytes and trapping them in vessels
Lipid A in the outer membrane causing neutropenia
Protein A binding the Fc portion of opsonizing IgG
Superantigen-driven destruction of marrow neutrophil precursors
approach: Identify the organism: large, boxcar-shaped gram-positive rods in a deep contaminated wound are Clostridium perfringens.
Recall its main toxin: alpha toxin is a phospholipase C (lecithinase) that breaks down the lecithin of cell membranes.
Apply it to leukocytes: the toxin destroys neutrophils in the tissue and makes them clump inside small vessels, so few reach the wound.
questions.why: Clostridium perfringens alpha toxin is a phospholipase C that hydrolyzes lecithin in cell membranes, lysing muscle cells, red cells, platelets, and leukocytes. At lower concentrations it also activates platelets and neutrophils so they aggregate and stick inside vessels (leukostasis). Neutrophils are destroyed in the tissue or never leave the vessels, so the dying muscle shows few inflammatory cells. This is a classic feature of gas gangrene and contrasts with the heavy neutrophil infiltrate of most bacterial infections.
whyNot: Correct.
Lipid A is the toxic part of lipopolysaccharide in gram-negative outer membranes. Clostridium perfringens is gram-positive and has no outer membrane.
Protein A binds the Fc region of IgG and blocks opsonization. It is a Staphylococcus aureus virulence factor, and staphylococci are cocci in clusters.
Superantigens activate T cells broadly and cause toxic shock syndrome, made by Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes. They do not explain absent neutrophils in clostridial myonecrosis.

questions.stem: Over the next 6 hours his urine turns dark red-brown, and his hematocrit falls from 44% to 29% without visible bleeding. Which of the following additional findings is most likely?
options: Positive Coombs test from IgG coating red cells
Positive Coombs test from complement fixed on red cells
Negative Coombs test with toxin lysis of red cells
Negative Coombs test with low red cell CD55 and CD59
approach: Recognize the finding: a sudden fall in hematocrit with dark urine means massive intravascular hemolysis.
Link it to the disease: in clostridial myonecrosis, circulating alpha toxin breaks down red cell membranes directly.
Because no antibody or complement is involved, the direct Coombs test is negative.
questions.why: Severe gas gangrene can release enough alpha toxin into the blood to cause massive intravascular hemolysis. The toxin's phospholipase activity destroys red cell membranes directly, so free hemoglobin causes red-brown urine and the hematocrit drops quickly. No antibody or complement coats the cells, so the direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is negative. Hemolysis, shock, and rapid spread with crepitus and bronze skin are hallmarks of clostridial infection.
whyNot: IgG on red cells is warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, as in SLE or chronic lymphocytic leukemia, which causes mainly extravascular hemolysis with spherocytes.
Complement on red cells is typical of cold agglutinin disease or some drug reactions. Toxin lysis does not depend on antibody or complement.
Correct.
Low CD55 and CD59 is paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, an acquired stem cell disorder with complement-mediated hemolysis. It does not develop suddenly with a wound infection.

questions.stem: Before surgery, the pressure in the anterior compartment of the thigh is 38 mm Hg (normal under 10). His blood pressure is 88/56 mm Hg, and the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are palpable. Which of the following best explains the ischemia of the quadriceps muscles?
options: Femoral arterial inflow stops once tissue pressure exceeds 30 mm Hg
A perfusion gradient near 18 mm Hg cannot keep capillaries open
Gas bubbles occlude the femoral artery within the adductor canal
Bullet fragments directly compress the profunda femoris artery
approach: Calculate the perfusion gradient: diastolic pressure minus compartment pressure is 56 minus 38, or 18 mm Hg.
Recall the threshold: a gradient under about 30 mm Hg is too low for capillary flow and calls for fasciotomy.
Notice that distal pulses are present, which shows that the large arteries are still open.
questions.why: Swelling of necrotic, infected muscle inside an unyielding fascial compartment raises tissue pressure. Muscle perfusion depends on the difference between arterial pressure and tissue pressure. When diastolic pressure minus compartment pressure falls below about 30 mm Hg, capillaries and venules collapse and the muscle becomes ischemic. Hypotension, as in this septic patient, makes the gradient smaller at any given compartment pressure. Arterial pressure is still far higher than tissue pressure, so distal pulses stay palpable.
whyNot: Large arteries stay open at compartment pressures in this range because arterial pressure is much higher. His palpable distal pulses show that inflow through the femoral artery continues.
Correct.
Gas forms in the infected muscle and soft tissue. It does not occlude the femoral artery, and his distal pulses are present.
Retained fragments can injure an artery, but a direct compression would not explain the high compartment pressure. The ischemia here comes from the pressure in the compartment.

questions.stem: Type II necrotizing fasciitis was included in the differential diagnosis. Which of the following findings at surgery would most support that diagnosis over this patient's condition?
options: Gas tracking through the soft tissue planes
Dark, noncontractile muscle that does not bleed when cut
Large gram-positive rods with few neutrophils on Gram stain
Necrotic fascia over pink, contractile, bleeding muscle
approach: Locate each disease: necrotizing fasciitis spreads along the fascia, while gas gangrene destroys the muscle itself.
Recall the organism of type II necrotizing fasciitis: Streptococcus pyogenes, a gram-positive coccus in chains that does not usually make gas.
Choose the finding that shows dead fascia with healthy muscle beneath it.
questions.why: Necrotizing fasciitis is a rapidly spreading infection of the subcutaneous tissue and deep fascia. Type II is caused by Streptococcus pyogenes, often in healthy people after minor trauma. At surgery the fascia is gray and necrotic and separates easily, but the muscle underneath is usually viable: pink, contractile, and bleeding. In clostridial myonecrosis the muscle itself is dead, dark, noncontractile, and does not bleed. Both can cause severe pain, rapid spread, and shock.
whyNot: Gas in tissue planes is typical of clostridial infection and of type I polymicrobial necrotizing fasciitis. Streptococcus pyogenes alone usually does not produce gas.
Dead, noncontractile muscle that does not bleed is myonecrosis, the defining finding of gas gangrene.
Large gram-positive rods with few neutrophils describe Clostridium perfringens. Type II necrotizing fasciitis shows gram-positive cocci in chains.
Correct.

dx: Fournier gangrene (type I necrotizing fasciitis) in a man with diabetes
case: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department because of a 3-day history of worsening pain and swelling of the scrotum and perineum. He stopped taking his medications 6 months ago. His temperature is 39.1 °C (102.4 °F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 94/60 mm Hg. The scrotum and perineum are swollen, with dusky purple patches, foul-smelling drainage, and crepitus. Erythema and induration extend onto the lower anterior abdominal wall. Serum glucose concentration is 410 mg/dL (normal 70 to 100), hemoglobin A1c is 11.4% (normal under 5.7%), and leukocyte count is 24,600/mm3 (normal 4,500 to 11,000). CT shows gas along the fascial planes of the scrotum, perineum, and lower abdominal wall. Diagnosis: Fournier gangrene (type I necrotizing fasciitis).

questions.stem: Tissue obtained at debridement is sent for aerobic and anaerobic culture. Which of the following results is most likely?
options: Streptococcus pyogenes growing as the only organism
Clostridium perfringens growing as the only organism
Mixed gram-negative rods, enterococci, and anaerobes
Staphylococcus aureus growing as the only organism
approach: Classify the infection: necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum in a man with poorly controlled diabetes is type I (Fournier gangrene).
Recall that type I is polymicrobial, caused by facultative bowel and skin organisms working together with anaerobes.
Gas on CT and foul drainage fit a mixed infection with anaerobes.
questions.why: Type I necrotizing fasciitis is polymicrobial. It usually affects people with diabetes, obesity, or recent surgery, and the perineal form is Fournier gangrene. Cultures grow a mix of facultative organisms, such as Escherichia coli and other Enterobacterales, enterococci, and streptococci, along with anaerobes such as Bacteroides. The facultative organisms use up oxygen, which lets the anaerobes grow, and the mixed metabolism produces gas and foul-smelling discharge.
whyNot: Streptococcus pyogenes alone causes type II necrotizing fasciitis, usually of a limb in a previously healthy person. The perineal site and diabetes point to type I.
Clostridium perfringens alone causes gas gangrene, a myonecrosis after deep contaminated wounds. Fournier gangrene is a mixed infection of the fascia.
Correct.
Staphylococcus aureus can cause single-organism necrotizing infections, but it is not the usual cause of Fournier gangrene. Foul drainage and gas point to anaerobes.

topics: Type I versus type II necrotizing fasciitis

questions.stem: Type II necrotizing fasciitis, by contrast, is usually caused by a single beta-hemolytic organism that grows in chains. Which of the following virulence factors of that organism most directly allows it to resist phagocytosis?
options: Streptokinase converting plasminogen to plasmin
Hyaluronidase breaking down connective tissue matrix
Protein A binding the Fc region of IgG
M protein limiting C3b deposition on the bacterium
approach: Identify the organism: beta-hemolytic gram-positive cocci in chains causing type II necrotizing fasciitis are Streptococcus pyogenes.
Separate its virulence factors by job: some help it spread through tissue, and one helps it avoid being eaten by phagocytes.
M protein blocks opsonization by complement, so it is the antiphagocytic factor.
questions.why: Streptococcus pyogenes uses M protein as its main defense against phagocytosis. M protein binds host regulators such as factor H and C4b-binding protein, which limits deposition of the opsonin C3b on the bacterial surface, so neutrophils cannot easily grab it. Antibodies against a specific M protein type give type-specific immunity. Hyaluronidase and streptokinase help the organism spread along fascial planes, and pyrogenic exotoxins act as superantigens that cause streptococcal toxic shock.
whyNot: Streptokinase activates plasminogen, which dissolves fibrin and helps the organism spread. It does not protect the bacterium from phagocytes.
Hyaluronidase digests hyaluronic acid in connective tissue and helps the infection spread. It is a spreading factor, not an antiphagocytic factor.
Protein A is a Staphylococcus aureus factor that binds IgG by its Fc region. Streptococcus pyogenes uses M protein instead.
Correct.

questions.stem: The infection has spread from the perineum and scrotum onto the lower anterior abdominal wall, but the thighs are spared. Continuity of which of the following fascial layers best explains this pattern of spread?
options: Colles fascia with Scarpa fascia of the abdominal wall
Camper fascia with the fascia lata of the thigh
Transversalis fascia with internal spermatic fascia
External oblique aponeurosis with the inguinal ligament
approach: Locate the infection: Fournier gangrene spreads in the superficial perineal space, beneath the membranous layer of perineal fascia (Colles fascia).
Recall the layers of the abdominal wall: the superficial fascia has a fatty layer (Camper) and a membranous layer (Scarpa).

Colles fascia continues as the dartos fascia of the scrotum and the Scarpa fascia of the abdominal wall, but it is fused to the fascia lata just below the inguinal ligament, so infection cannot pass into the thigh.
questions.why: The membranous layer of superficial fascia forms one continuous sheet: Scarpa fascia on the lower anterior abdominal wall, dartos fascia around the penis and scrotum, and Colles fascia in the perineum. Laterally it fuses with the fascia lata of the thigh just below the inguinal ligament and attaches to the ischiopubic rami, and posteriorly it fuses with the perineal membrane. Fluid or infection under this layer, such as urine from a ruptured spongy urethra or Fournier gangrene, can rise onto the abdominal wall but cannot enter the thighs or the anal triangle.
whyNot: Correct.
Camper fascia is the fatty superficial layer. It continues into the superficial fat of the thigh and perineum and does not form the barrier that confines this spread.
Transversalis fascia does continue as the internal spermatic fascia, but this deep layer lies inside the abdominal wall muscles and is not the plane of Fournier gangrene.
The external oblique aponeurosis forms the inguinal ligament and the external spermatic fascia. It lies deep to the superficial fascia where this infection spreads.

topics: Layers of the anterior abdominal wall

questions.stem: He also has a black, shriveled left fifth toe that is sharply demarcated from the adjacent normal skin, with no swelling or drainage. The dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are absent on the left. Which of the following best describes the process in this toe?
options: Liquefactive necrosis from superimposed bacterial infection
Coagulative necrosis from arterial insufficiency
Caseous necrosis from a granulomatous infection
Fat necrosis from enzymatic release of lipase
approach: Read the description: a black, dry, shriveled toe with a sharp border and no drainage is dry gangrene.
Link it to the cause: absent pedal pulses mean arterial occlusion and ischemia.
Ischemia of a solid tissue without infection causes coagulative necrosis.
questions.why: Dry gangrene is ischemic coagulative necrosis of a limb part, usually a toe, after arterial occlusion. Without bacterial infection, the dead tissue dries and mummifies, turns black, and is sharply separated from living tissue. Diabetes and peripheral artery disease raise the risk because of atherosclerosis and small vessel disease, and neuropathy delays recognition of injury. If bacteria invade, liquefactive necrosis is added and the lesion becomes wet gangrene, which is swollen, moist, and poorly demarcated.
whyNot: Liquefactive necrosis from infection defines wet gangrene, which is swollen, moist, and poorly demarcated. This toe is dry and sharply demarcated.
Correct.
Caseous necrosis is the cheesy necrosis of tuberculosis and some fungal infections. It does not explain an ischemic toe.
Fat necrosis occurs in acute pancreatitis or after trauma to fatty tissue such as the breast. It is not the result of arterial occlusion in a toe.
